TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (“ALJs”):
       The Segment K13/K51 Landowners timely file their Initial Post-Hearing Brief in this
proceeding and would respectfully show as follows:

                                      I. INTRODUCTION
       This IS NOT an ordinary case. This is an extraordinary case. The proposed transmission
line at the center of this proceeding is not an ordinary transmission line. It is one of the new import
paths’ 765-kV “backbone” transmission lines—by far the largest lines ever to be constructed in
Texas. The transmission line will include 200’ ROWs and massive steel towers that will dominate
the surrounding countryside for generations to come. The proposed location of this line is not
ordinary, either. This line is planned to be constructed through the heart of Texas’ famed Hill
Country, one of the most beautiful, historic and iconic parts of Texas. This line will directly impact
two of Texas’ most iconic rivers, the Colorado River and the San Saba River. The line, depending
on where it is built, could also impact two very important state parks, Colorado Bend State Park
and Post Oak Ridge State Park, and a historic ranch that was established before the Civil War and
continues to operate to this day.
       The level of public participation in this case is not ordinary. It is extraordinary. There were

                                                  3
 over 800 intervenors filing either direct testimony or statements of position in this docket over a
period of only seven weeks. At last check, there were over 6,200 individual filings in the PUC
Interchange. The Hearing on the Merits lasted five days. There were so many parties involved that
cross-examination of intervenor witnesses was necessarily limited to three minutes per party.
        The extraordinary facts of this case account for the extraordinary level of concern the
community has regarding the impact of the transmission line on the Hill Country. Proponents of
Route 894 rely heavily on over-weighted factors of cost, length, habitable structures and
paralleling to justify the use of Route 894. The law is clear that none of these factors is dispositive.
These parties downplay or outright ignore the other factors set forth in the law. All factors must
be considered and balanced based on the full record, rather than defaulting to a mere routing table
exercise.
        As will be further discussed in this brief, an oversimplified ‘cost, habitable structures,
paralleling equals “best meets” route’ analysis fails to account for the unique circumstances present
in this case and should not be the end of the inquiry here. Former PUC Chairman, Barry
Smitherman, testified in this case, “[t]hese cases are challenging. They are personal for the
landowners and the affected communities. It is important that the Commission get these cases
right. Part of getting it right means following the law and evaluating all of the statutory and rule
factors in a reasoned way. While it is tempting to reduce the analysis to a numerical exercise that
gives a feeling of objectivity, doing so would not be consistent with the public service role of the
Commission. The ultimate goal is to find a resolution that is least harmful on the community and
the property owners involved while still complying with the statute and applicable rules to allow
needed projects to be built.”1 That is precisely the approach requested here: apply the existing laws
and Commission rules faithfully with full consideration of the parks, rivers, viewsheds,
environmental resources, historic ranchlands, and affected communities shown in this record to
select the route that best meets all of the relevant criteria.
        There are eight (8) leading “routes of interest” in this proceeding.2 These routes are Route
296, Route 392, Route 410, Route 487, Route 572, Route 891, Route 894, and Route Cherokee
Creek G or “CCG.”3 Of these eight routes, only one avoids adversely impacting Colorado Bend

along previously established infrastructure corridors to minimize new disturbance on these
rivers—that route is Route CCG. These important aspects of Route CCG cannot be overstated
given the extraordinary facts of this case. Other strong southern route options are Routes 572 and
296. Routes 572 and 296 carry forward most of the benefits of Route CCG, but essentially
exchange a less desirable crossing of the San Saba River for some cost savings. The Segment
K13/K51 Landowners believe Route CCG, Route 572 or Route 296 should be the “best meets”
route in this case.
        Although the Segment K13/K51 Landowners strongly advocate for a “southern route” in
this case (i.e., Route CCG, Route 572, Route 296), if the ALJs and Commission determine a
southern route is not acceptable, a “northern route” (i.e., Route 392 or Route 410) should be
selected. These northern routes both avoid impacts to Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak
Ridge State Park, and they both utilize a crossing of the Colorado River along an existing
infrastructure corridor. As reflected in the record of this proceeding, Zach Brady’s clients have
made persuasive arguments in favor of Route 392, and several other parties and experts support
Routes 392 and 410. Route 410, which is identical to Route 392 except in the eastern study area,
carries forward many of the benefits of Route 392, but exchanges a slightly higher cost for a
reduction of habitable structure impacts.
        Both the southern routes and the northern routes are superior to the central routes (i.e.,
Routes 894, 487, and 891). The central routes, while slightly better than the other routes on certain
quantitative routing factors, all adversely impact both Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak
Ridge State Park in significant fashion, and fail to mitigate impacts to both the Colorado River and
the San Saba River. The overall negative impact to all Texans, both now and for generations to
come, is greatest along these central routes. The question is whether it is worth imposing those
avoidable impacts when other reasonable routes are available that better protect the very heart of
Texas, our iconic rivers, natural resources and state parks. Under the Commission’s ordinary
routing framework, the answer should be no.
        This is NOT an ordinary case. But the rules are ordinary, and they are sufficient. When
these rules are applied to the extraordinary facts in the record, Route CCG is the route that best
meets the Commission’s criteria.

                    II. JURISDICTION AND DEADLINE FOR DECISION

        The Commission has jurisdiction over this proceeding under PURA Sections 14.001,
32.001, 37.051, 37.053, 37.054, and 37.056. SOAH has jurisdiction to conduct a hearing on the
merits and to issue a PFD under PURA Section 14.053 and Tex. Gov’t Code Section 2003.049.
PURA Section 37.057 requires the Commission to act on the Joint Applicants’ application within
180 days after the Joint Applicants’ filed their application.

                             III. PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES

Preliminary Order also identified certain issues not to be addressed, including compensation for
rights-of-way or for condemnation.5

E. ROUTE (ISSUE NO. 8)

      8.      Weighing the factors set forth in PURA §37.056(c) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code
§25.101(b)(3)(B), which proposed transmission-line route is the best alternative?

       Upon weighing the factors set forth in PURA §37.056(c) and 16 Tex. Admin. Code

                                                 7
 §25.101(b)(3)(B), Route Cherokee Creek G or “CCG” is the best alternative. Routes 572 and 296
are also reasonable southern routes supported by the record. Routes 410 and 392 are reasonable
northern alternatives. PURA §37.056(c) requires the Commission to consider the effect of its
decision on community values; recreational and park areas; historical and aesthetic values;
environmental integrity; and the probable improvement of service or lowering of costs to
consumers.7 In implementing PURA §37.056(c), the Commission established regulatory criteria,
requiring consideration of the PURA criteria, engineering constraints, and costs in “rout[ing the
line] to the extent possible to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners
unless grid reliability and security dictate otherwise.”8 The Commission’s rules further provide
that consideration must be given to:
         (i)      whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible rights-of-way for electric
                  facilities, including the use of vacant positions on existing multiple-circuit
                  transmission lines;
         (ii)     whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-of-way,
                  including roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of-way;
         (iii)    whether the routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features; and
         (iv)     whether the routes conform with the policy of prudent avoidance.9

         Nothing in either PURA or the Commission’s rules dictates that any of these factors is
more important or more relevant than any other factor. In other words, there is no “primary” factor
to be considered above all others. As the court held in Dunn v. Public Utility Commission of Texas,
“The plain language of [PUC SUBST. R. §25.101(b)(3)] grants the PUC the authority to consider
and weigh a variety of factors—engineering constraints, costs, grid reliability and security, along
with the criteria in PURA §37.056 …. No one factor is dispositive.”10 In this extraordinary case
routing a transmission line through the heart of the Texas Hill Country, no one factor is dispositive
and no one route is superior on all the relevant routing criteria. Based on a careful and thoughtful
balancing of all the required criteria, Route CCG is superior to all other route options including
but not limited to Routes 894 and 487 and all other central routes.

       i. Community values; PURA §37.056(c)(4)(A)
        The term “community values” is included as a factor for consideration, but the term is not
formally defined by statute or in the Commission’s rules. The Commission has viewed the term
“community values” as “a shared appreciation of an area or other natural resource by a national,
regional, or local community.”11 Commission decisions also define adverse effects on community
values as “those aspects of a proposed project that would significantly alter the use, enjoyment, or
intrinsic value attached to an important area or resource by a community.”12 However, these are
not the only possible definitions. Community values are certainly not limited to numbers on a
routing table.
        Community values always deserve serious consideration, but even more so given the
impacts this project will have on all Texans for generations to come, our prized Texas Hill Country,
two pristine state parks, and ecologically-sensitive major rivers and tributaries.


State Parks
        Although many parties acknowledge the importance of parks and recreational areas, among
the Routes of Interest, only the southern routes (i.e., CCG, 572, 296) and the northern routes (i.e.,
392, 410) go beyond acknowledging those resources and actually protect them. The central routes
(i.e., Routes 894, 487, and 891) do not.

more than 400 caves due to the limestone terrain, making it significant for cave exploration. In
addition to its caves, visitors are drawn to features like Gorman Falls and the scenic beauty of the
Colorado River.14 Colorado Bend State Park is described by former Executive Director of TPWD,

Iconic Texas Rivers
        The Commission should select a route that crosses the Colorado River at Link J31. The
location of the Colorado River crossing is one of the most important routing decisions in this case.
The Colorado River is not merely another stream crossing to be counted in a raw total.73 It is a
major hydrologic, biological, scenic, and recreational feature of the study area.74 A crossing of the
Colorado River may affect not only the river channel itself, but also the associated riparian
corridor, adj acent woodland, wildlife movement, scenic quality, and recreational experience in the
surrounding area.75
        Three routes on the Routes of Interest Map cross the Colorado River at J31: Route CCG,
Route 572, and Route 296.76 That convergence of support for the river crossing at J31 is important.
While the parties supporting those routes do not agree on every routing issue, they do agree that
J31 is an appropriate Colorado River crossing.

contested crossings at Jl 1, J22, or J26. Link J31 is farther from Colorado Bend State Park and Post
Oak Ridge State Park,77 it consolidates the river crossing near existing linear infrastructure,78 and
